newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore electronics output seen rising 10-15 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore electronics output seen rising 10-15 pct.

text.p: Singapore's electronics sector is expected to grow 10 to 15 percent this year after unusually slow single-digit growth in 1996, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Monday.
"In 1997, we see 10 to 15 percent in output growth for the electronic sector," Liow Voon Kheong, EDB's head of electronics, industry development division, told reporters at a briefing.

"We're still quite optimistic that growth will continue with forecast world electronics growth at around 6-8 percent," said Lai Yeow Hin, EDB's head of electronics systems, industry development division.
The projected growth is in line with the expectations of analysts who saw most of the growth coming in the second half.
The EDB said the electronics sector grew nine percent in 1996 with output of S$63.1 billion (US$45.1 billion) -- the first time in five years that it had only achieved single digit growth.

The electronics industry, excluding the electrical sector, drew fixed asset investment commitments of S$3.29 billion last year, an increase of 30 percent over 1995, EDB said. The semiconductor sector makes up 64 percent of the investment commitment.
In 1996, the data storage sector, which includes disk drive and CD-ROM drive manufacturers, grew a record 29 percent to S$18.3 billion.
The semiconductor sector inched up three percent to S$12.08 billion.
Consumer electronics plunged 20 percent to S$4.97 billion.
EDB said Singapore would strive for a better balance in the industry to "negate the industry's boom and bust cycle".
Liow said Singapore would still promote the semiconductor industry despite the tough environment where dynamic random access memory (DRAM) prices have dropped 75 percent in the past year.
"We will build on the strength of the projects we have managed to attract into Singapore -- semiconductors, computer peripherals, multimedia products."
More focus would be given to other key components of sectors that were new to Singapore like disk media and flat panel displays, he said.
He said consumer electronic companies were shifting into new product areas like telecommunications, the full impact of which had not been felt in 1996.
Liow said Singapore expected to attract two new wafer fabrication projects in 1997. Wafer fabs etch circuits onto silicon wafers that are cut up to form computer chips.
There are currently three wafer fabrication companies operating four plants in Singapore with at least three more plants in the process of being built.
Volume of output from wafer fabs grew 30 percent in 1996 over 1995, EDB said. Revenue from wafer fabs was flat at S$1.5-S$1.6 billion in 1996 out of a total semiconductor output of S$12 billion.
